# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](../packs/) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does.
- **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md](../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`.
- **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc.
- **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control.
- **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.)
- **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of.
- **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes.
- **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked.
# Claudinite — active-pack guidance

The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand.

<!-- pack:basics -->
# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.

Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.

Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix.

1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.

Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.

When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.

When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."

Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.

Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.

Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.

When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.

An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

---

<!-- pack:tidy-repo -->
# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy

The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the
pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is
the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills
([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).

The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
  ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites
**its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body
rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the
three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body.

# Claudinite — the canon's own non-portable working rules

This is the Claudinite home repo's own local pack: the capture surface for lessons that are
**specific to working on the canon itself** and would not make sense mounted into a consuming
project. Portable lessons — anything true for repos beyond this one — belong in the shared canon
under `packs/`/`skills/` instead (proposed by PR, or lifted by the promote stage).

The growth lifecycle writes here automatically: the `growth-extract` and `conversation-extract`
daily tasks route the canon's own non-portable lessons into this pack (each at the local
promotion ladder's strongest mechanism — a check where the rule is deterministic, otherwise terse
prose below).

## Standing owner decisions — settled, do not re-litigate

- **`canon-curation` lives in `.claudinite/local/packs/`, not `packs/`** (owner decision,
  2026-07-19). The canon home's curation duties are Claudinite-maintaining-Claudinite —
  project-specific content on the home's own capture surface. Do not propose moving it back, and
  do not describe the move as open or provisional.
- **Local-pack `run_daily` scheduling is ON — the fleet's default path** (same decision). The
  planner reads every member's local-pack daily descriptors by default; never reintroduce an
  "experimental / not enabled" framing or an opt-in seam for it.
- **Packs-tree segregation is barriers configuration only.** Any rule about what the `packs/`
  tree may reference is expressed by declaring/configuring the `barriers` pack (contributed
  edges, `siblings`/`scope` capabilities — extend barriers generically if a capability is
  missing). Never write standalone code that checks packs-tree segregation.
- **A `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md` records the mechanism only** (owner decision, 2026-07-23,
  #420). Status, phase tracking, in-flight-PR reconciliation and remaining work live in that
  initiative's tracking issue (agent-preprocessing → #394); a phased plan lives in the sibling
  `MIGRATION.md`. Don't reintroduce a status / open-questions / remaining-work section there.
- **Multi-session work hands off through the tracking issue, never a prepared prompt** (owner
  correction, 2026-07-23). The owner's opener is `continue work on #<n>`, so state not written
  into the issue is lost. Before ending a session on unfinished work, update the issue and let
  the session summary be a pointer to it — never compose a bespoke "pick up from here" prompt.
- **The canon never knows which repos consume it — fleet-wide aggregation is Sheepdog's domain**
  (owner correction, 2026-07-28, #520). Designing anything that spans repos, the tempting shape is
  a member list (or a "fleet" task) living in the canon. It doesn't go here: the canon carries only
  **mechanisms exercised on itself**, and the knowledge of *which* repos exist stays in the
  **Sheepdog** repo and its pack, which enumerates members at runtime from its own
  `.claudinite-checks.json` entry — exactly where `fleet-census` and `fleet-freshness` already keep
  it. So a cross-repo feature splits in two: a self-contained per-repo half in the canon, and the
  aggregation half as a Sheepdog fleet task. **No repo list exists anywhere in canon code** — and a
  derived fleet artifact lands in Sheepdog as a daily **auto-merged PR of a `GENERATED` file**,
  never a direct commit to its `main`.
- **A pack default stays in the pack — don't ask it at adoption, don't write it into a member's
  config** (owner ruling, 2026-07-28, #527/#528). An adoption question whose recommended answer is
  right for nearly everyone is "bad noise": it taxes every adopting repo to re-state the default,
  and materializing that answer into `.claudinite-checks.json` freezes a copy that then drifts from
  the pack and has to be migrated. Keep the default in the pack's own code, ask nothing, and let the
  rare project that wants to differ add the setting by hand. Read config as *optional* — an unset
  key means "the default", never "misconfigured" (`retention_days` unset is precisely why the
  conversation-extract prune is skipped rather than failing).

## Canon-specific gotchas

- **Baselining backfill skips the home — hand-declare fleet-seeded packs here.** The nightly
  baselining that lands a `seededByDefault` pack (and canon-delivered declaration changes) on
  every member is gated `!isHome`, so the canon home is the one repo it never reaches: a newly
  seeded pack does *not* arrive here automatically — the home's own `.claudinite-checks.json`
  must be updated by hand in the same change that flips the seed. The natural drift-guard (a
  future check, once the home is clean) is: the home declares every `seededByDefault` non-local
  pack.
- **The home doesn't declare `git-github`, so its skills never mount — never conclude "no such
  skill" from `.claude/skills/`.** `mount-skills.mjs` filters on the *literal* declaration
  (`isActive(p, { packs: declared })`), not the `requires` closure `check_the_world.mjs` resolves,
  and the baselining that would normalize that closure into `.claudinite-checks.json` is the one
  thing gated `!isHome` — so `merge-to-main` and `git-github-advanced` are simply absent here.
  Read `packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` out of the tracked tree — the corpus *is* this repo,
  and an unmounted skill says nothing about whether its procedure applies. The seed-based
  drift-guard above would not catch this (`git-github` arrives by closure, never
  `seededByDefault`); a real one compares `resolveDeclaredPacks` against the literal declaration.
- **Never re-serialize a repo's JSON config to apply an edit — patch the text.** A round-trip
  rewrites what it wasn't asked to: Python's `json.dump` defaults to `ensure_ascii=True` (every
  non-ASCII character becomes a `\uXXXX` escape), and indent, key order and the trailing newline
  become the serializer's opinion. Nothing fails and tests stay green, so it rides onward. Edit
  JSON as anchored text; if you must round-trip, pin every lossy default and read the resulting
  diff before committing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `repo-text-sweeps`, where a
  `\uXXXX`-in-tracked-JSON check would carry it.)
- **Test git fixtures must commit with signing off.** `engine-tests/helpers.mjs`'s `makeRepo`
  overrides identity but not signing, so all 31 call sites route fixture commits through the
  signing service; when it degrades, each commit blocks on it and the suite leaks descriptors
  (~800 per full run against a 4096 cap) until `git commit` and `git push` fail process-wide.
  Commit with `git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit --no-gpg-sign`: signing a tmpdir throwaway
  buys nothing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `writing-tests`.)
- **A canon session with a consumer repo also in its sources will reach for the *consumer's*
  merge skill — merge by the skill of the repo you are merging into.** Canon work is routinely
  dual-repo (the canon plus the fleet member being piloted), and both repos ship a merge skill
  under different names — the canon's `packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/` and, say, GCEC's
  local `merge-and-ci`. The consumer's skill wins the match on name/description and is followed
  to the letter, so the canon-only steps in *its* recipe are silently skipped — repeatedly, the
  **post-merge conversation capture** (`node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue
  <n>`, the "After the merge" section of `merge-to-main`). So: before merging in a dual-repo
  session, resolve the merge skill **by target repo**, not by which skill matched first — and
  treat capture as part of the merge, not as an optional epilogue.
- **Fail-soft SessionStart steps hide their own breakage fleet-wide — test the emitted
  output, not the exit code.** Every `engine/pack_loader/` SessionStart step
  (`inject-pack-prose.mjs`, `mount-skills.mjs`, `env-requirements.mjs`) wraps its body in
  `try { ... } catch {}` so a broken loader never blocks a session. That fail-soft is deliberate,
  but it means a runtime fault — a wrong dynamic-import target, a renamed module — exits 0 and
  simply emits nothing: no error, no signal. And because the engine is vendored verbatim into
  every member, one canon regression silently disables that step across the whole fleet at once.
  So a step like this must be guarded by a regression test that runs the real script against a
  real corpus and asserts the **positive** effect — prose IS emitted — never merely that
  `status === 0` (which fail-soft makes meaningless); see
  `engine-tests/pack_loader/inject-pack-prose.test.mjs`.
- **The nightly self-refresh cannot repair the vendor-set computation — pin operational
  files against the REAL canon tree.** Baselining's converge re-runs
  `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.mjs` from canon HEAD, so a bug *in that computation* is
  the one class of canon regression that is not self-healing: every refresh faithfully
  reproduces it, and recovery is an out-of-band vendor refresh applied to each member by
  hand. So when the vendor set excludes by *pattern*, an operational file that matches
  needs a by-path whitelist (`VENDORED_ENGINE_DOCS`) **and** a regression test asserting
  against the real canon tree, not only a synthetic fixture: a fixture keeps proving the
  whitelist mechanism works while the live path silently drops out from under it (see the
  paired tests in `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.test.mjs`).
- **You cannot force a due slot by running the scheduler workflow by hand.** Dueness is
  stateless — a slot is due iff its time falls in `(last successful run, now]` — so a
  `workflow_dispatch` run outside the slot's window succeeds, prints `- no tasks due`, and
  does nothing. It looks like a healthy run. To exercise a task Action-side, invoke its
  worker directly, or move the slot hour in `taskScheduler` and wait for the cron.
- **A scheduled task is gated twice — prove a change through `planRun`, never through its own
  precondition.** `planRun` computes the due list *before* any precondition runs, so a task whose
  most-recent slot has already been run is never evaluated and never reads its signals at all. #513's
  forced-run override landed with every test driving the precondition (or the signal collector) directly
  and was inert on exactly the run it existed for — the mid-day manual trigger — because the due-list
  gate it never touched had already dropped the task (`evaluations: []`; fixed in #516). A test that
  starts *inside* the gate proves only "works once evaluated" and says nothing about whether the task
  ever gets there. Drive the real `planRun` from a deliberately **non-due** slot: that is the only shape
  that catches it.
- **Every due task in a run shares ONE checkout — an agentless worker must not touch it.** The
  scheduler runs the whole due list in a single working tree, so a worker that checks out a branch or
  leaves an index behind hands the next task a tree it did not expect, and a run that dies leaves the
  mess for whatever follows. A task whose output is a regenerated file lands it through
  `engine/scheduler/deliver-generated.mjs` — git plumbing against the fetched base tip, with HEAD, the
  index and the working tree untouched — and reads its prior state from that base rather than local
  HEAD, so stacked runs stay idempotent. (`basics/baselining`'s own deliver is the deliberate
  exception: it commits a whole working tree under the member's delivery preference.)
- **A code-search hit is evidence; a code-search miss is not — survey by reading each file.**
- **Derive the test file list from the tree — every hand-written glob here under-runs the suite.**
  There is no `package.json` and no test script, so each session invents its own incantation and
  silently verifies less than it thinks. Measured in this checkout: `node --test <dir>` does not
  recurse — it resolves the path as a module and dies with `Cannot find module`; bash `**` is not
  recursive without `globstar`, so `engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs` reaches
  **37 of 65** tracked test files. Four consecutive sessions (2026-07-26, #459/#452/#435/#468) each
  wrote a different command and reported 587, 690, 621 and 697 tests — three of them pushed after
  running a strict subset. Neither published list is authoritative either: `ci.yml`'s `tests=(…)`
  array omits `vendoring/*.test.mjs`, and `engine/checks/README.md`'s "as CI runs it" one-liner
  names `engine/test/`, `skills/` and `mount/`, none of which exist. So enumerate from git and let
  the count speak: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. (The drift-guard, once the array is
  clean: assert every tracked `*.test.mjs` is matched by `ci.yml`'s globs.)
- **A branch that waited overnight has lost its base *and* possibly its premise — re-verify the
  problem still exists on current `main`, unasked.** This repo merges its own scheduled-task PRs
  without a human, on top of multi-phase migrations that retire whole directories: measured on
  PR #465, `main` moved **14 commits in 13.7 hours** and one of them (#473, "retire `run_daily/`")
  *deleted the file the PR's diagnosis rested on* and had already landed most of its content. The
  branch rebased cleanly and the tests stayed green — the change was simply no longer the change to
  make, and the correct move was `git checkout -B <branch> origin/main` and re-applying only the
  surviving slice (9 files → 2). So syncing the base is not the check; the check is a **content**
  one: after `git fetch`, read what the new commits did to the surface you are changing and state
  whether the problem is still there, what the goal was, and what survives. Do this whenever you
  return to a paused branch, before presenting it — the owner should never have to ask "is this
  change still needed" (asked three times on #465 before it was volunteered).
- **`subscribe_pr_activity` blocks for minutes — subscribe once, and never as a way to "wait for
  CI".** It reads like a cheap registration, so a session calls it, gets no answer, and calls it
  again on the same PR. Measured in the #520 session (`2026-07-28T2208Z`): two consecutive calls on
  PR #524 cost **237s + 220s**, and a `send_later` check-in a further **101s** — **558s of that
  session's 841s of total tool wall-clock (66%)**, all pure idle, in a session whose actual work was
  153 tool calls. One subscription per PR is all there is to gain; a second adds nothing but the
  wait. When what you actually want is "is it green yet", read the check status directly and merge
  on the already-green result — don't buy the same notification twice.
- **The home has no `.claudinite/shared/` mount — machinery paths must accept both roots.** A
  consumer runs the vendored engine under `.claudinite/shared/engine/…` with packs under
  `.claudinite/(shared|local)/packs/…`; the home *is* the corpus and runs the same code from the
  repo root. So a path, regex, or workflow command written to the consumer mount shape works
  fleet-wide and fails on exactly this repo — the last place anyone exercises it, so the break
  surfaces late. Write the two-root form up front: make the `.claudinite/(shared|local)/` prefix
  optional in a pattern, and in a command probe for `.claudinite/shared/` first, falling back to
  the repo root.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

content.content:
1	# Skill-usage metrics — design
2	
3	Status: **agreed** (owner decisions recorded in §10; design review in the
4	2026-07-28 session). Refs #520. This document describes the **final state**
5	only; there is no migration plan — the rollout self-converges through the
6	existing machinery (the nightly vendored-canon refresh carries the code, a
7	baselining-applied migration note registers the hook), and the one ordering
8	constraint (§3.4) is satisfied by shipping the capture changes in one PR.
9	
10	The problem: skills are mounted per repo, but mounting only puts a name and a
11	one-line description into the session's system prompt — actually *loading* the
12	skill is model discretion, and nothing records whether it ever happens. The
13	only evidence is the session transcript, which is ephemeral (and, once captured
14	to the `conversation-logs` branch, deleted at retention). So the promotion
15	ladder's rung-4/rung-5 call — skill vs prose — has no empirical feedback: a
16	skill whose trigger never fires is indistinguishable from one that fires daily,
17	and a "skill" that fires in every session (rules wearing a skill's clothes) is
18	indistinguishable from a genuinely activity-scoped one.
19	
20	The same blind spot covers the **conformance checks**, from the other side. A
21	check that fails is a win: the finding reaches the session through the Stop
22	hook and the agent corrects before the work leaves the branch. Nothing counts
23	those corrections either — so "is this rule earning its place" and "is
24	enforcement even running" are as unanswerable as "does this skill ever load".
25	The checks ride the same pipeline, and §4.1 is where they are counted.
26	
27	The shape: session transcripts already record every skill invocation, and the
28	check runners leave readable marks in them too. Capture already ships
29	transcripts to each repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch at merge time.
30	This design (a) enriches capture with a best-effort session-end event, (b) adds
31	a deterministic daily **fold** in each repo that counts skill loads, check
32	activations and failures, and activity denominators from the live logs into a
33	small tracked aggregate, and (c) adds a **fleet sweep** in the sheepdog pack
34	that recomputes a fleet-wide aggregate from the members' files into the
35	fleet-enforcer repo. Every stage is deterministic code — no agent judgment
36	anywhere in the pipeline.
37	
38	```
39	transcript ──(merge capture / SessionEnd capture)──▶ conversation-logs branch
40	    conversation-logs ──(usage-fold, per repo, daily)──▶ .claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json
41	    member usage files ──(fleet-usage, sheepdog, daily)──▶ usage-fleet.GENERATED.json (enforcer repo)
42	```
43	
44	---
45	
46	## 1. Where knowledge lives — the placement rule
47	
48	The canon knows **mechanisms**, never repos. The fleet-enforcer repo knows
49	**the fleet**. Each member knows **itself**.
50	
51	| piece | home | knows about |
52	|---|---|---|
53	| capture (merge + SessionEnd) | `grow_with_claudinite` pack (canon) | its own session, its own logs branch |
54	| `usage-fold` (daily) | `grow_with_claudinite/tasks/usage-fold/` (canon) | its own logs branch, its own aggregate file |
55	| `fleet-usage` (daily) | `sheepdog/tasks/fleet-usage/` (canon pack; runs only where sheepdog is declared) | nothing hardcoded — members enumerated at runtime from the sheepdog config (`{ owner, kind, exclude, canonRepo }`) via `fleet-api.mjs`, exactly as `fleet-census` does |
56	| the fleet aggregate | the fleet-enforcer repo's default branch | — |
57	
58	No repo list exists in any code, canon or otherwise. The member set is derived
59	where it already is today for the census and freshness sweeps.
60	
61	## 2. Sources of truth, and what is derived
62	
63	- The **transcript** is the source of truth for what happened in a session.
64	- The **`conversation-logs` branch** is a byte-faithful (scrubbed) window onto
65	  transcripts, retained `retention_days` (§3).
66	- The **per-repo aggregate** is derived: day rows are a pure function of the
67	  live logs; week rows are append-once sums of closed day rows (§5).
68	- The **fleet aggregate** is derived: a pure function of the current member
69	  files, fully recomputed each run (§6). Never store what you can derive —
70	  the fleet file keeps full (week × repo × skill) grain precisely so every
71	  coarser view remains derivable from it.
72	
73	Both aggregate files are `GENERATED`-named and machine-written only, under the
74	canon's GENERATED-file discipline (regenerated, never hand-edited).
75	
76	## 3. Capture — two events, one idempotent mechanism
77	
78	### 3.1 The delta contract (existing, now pinned by tests)
79	
80	`capture-log.mjs` keys on the **session id**: every capture refetches the
81	branch tip, finds all prior `*--<sessionId>.jsonl` files (whatever event or
82	issue produced them), takes the max entry timestamp across them, and pushes
83	only the entries strictly after it. Zero delta ⇒ no file, no commit, no push.
84	This makes double-writing safe **by construction** — any two capture events for
85	one session chain into disjoint files — and it is the property the SessionEnd
86	hook (§3.3) relies on, so it is pinned by dedicated tests (repeat capture of an
87	unchanged transcript produces nothing; a post-merge tail produces exactly the
88	tail).
89	
90	One file therefore maps 1:1 to a **capture event**, not to a merge.
91	
92	### 3.2 No-issue captures: `issue-0`
93	
94	The filename stays `<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`, with **`0` meaning
95	"no associated issue"**. The filename regex, the retention prune, and the
96	scheduler's `conversationLogs` signal already accept `0` — only the CLI's
97	argument validation refuses it, and that is the whole change. Keeping the
98	filename shape identical is deliberate: any *new* shape would be invisible to
99	the prune and become immortal. `conversation-extract` treats an `issue-0` file
100	as having no issue to post its exchange summary on; everything else about its
101	two-pass lifecycle is unchanged.
102	
103	### 3.3 The SessionEnd hook — best effort, fail-soft
104	
105	A `SessionEnd` hook (`engine/hooks/session-end-command.mjs`, registered in the
106	consumer's `.claude/settings.json` like its siblings) runs capture with
107	`--issue 0`. Properties:
108	
109	- **SessionEnd, not Stop.** Stop fires at every turn end (and already runs the
110	  conformance checks); capturing there would push to the orphan branch once per
111	  turn and shred the branch into per-turn files. SessionEnd fires once.
112	- **Best effort, and that is enough.** A container reclaimed by timeout never
113	  fires it. Every firing strictly enriches the record (non-merging sessions,
114	  and the post-merge tail of merging ones); every miss leaves exactly today's
115	  behaviour. No correctness anywhere depends on the hook having fired.
116	- **Fail-soft.** It swallows every error, logs the attempt via `hooklog`, and
117	  must never block a session from ending. Absent `grow_with_claudinite` in the
118	  repo's declared packs, it exits without acting.
119	- Scrubbing is the existing capture scrub, unchanged — the hook adds a capture
120	  *event*, not a new write path.
121	
122	### 3.4 Ordering constraint
123	
124	The idempotence tests and the `issue-0` relaxation must be in the canon before
125	the hook registration reaches any member — an old `conversation-extract` would
126	try to comment on issue `#0`. Shipping all of §3 in one canon PR satisfies
127	this; the baselining task refreshes a member's mount before applying migration
128	notes, so a member can never run the hook against a stale capture script.
129	
130	## 4. Counting — one tested function per question
131	
132	All counting happens in the fold worker (§5), in exported, individually tested
133	functions. The capture path computes nothing.
134	
135	- **`skillLoads`** (per skill name): `Skill` tool_use entries, plus user-typed
136	  `/command` entries whose name matches a skill mounted in this repo (the
137	  mounted set comes from the pack registry — `loadPacks()` — not from the
138	  gitignored `.claude/skills/` mounts). Built-in CLI commands (`/model`,
139	  `/clear`, …) never match. Sidechain (subagent) streams are included — a
140	  subagent loading a skill is a load.
141	- **`captures`**: files folded (capture events). **`merges`**: the subset with
142	  issue > 0. Once the SessionEnd hook exists, these differ — the split exists
143	  from day one so no consumer ever reads an ambiguous column.
144	- **`sessions`**: distinct session ids among the bucket's captures (one
145	  session can capture more than once).
146	- **`userMessages`**: genuine human turns — user-role entries that are neither
147	  tool results nor scheduled-task/automated firings (the transcript marks
148	  these). This heuristic is the most fragile line in the design, so it lives
149	  in one function with fixtures for each entry shape it excludes.
150	- **`userCommands`**: user-typed `/command` entries, all of them — the
151	  cleanest "explicit asks" workload measure.
152	
153	Stated overlap: a typed `/merge-to-main` counts in both `userCommands` and
154	`skillLoads` — one event, two axes, both true.
155	
156	### 4.1 Check activations — and, above all, check *failures*
157	
158	Skills are half the picture. The conformance checks are the other half, and the
159	more valuable half: a check that **fails is a win**. The finding lands back in
160	the session through the Stop hook and the agent corrects before the work
161	leaves the branch — so "how often did the checks catch something" is a direct
162	measure of what the corpus is worth, and "which rule caught it" is the most
163	actionable number in the whole pipeline.
164	
165	Neither runner writes a metrics file, so both are counted off the marks they
166	already leave in the transcript. There are exactly three, each verified against
167	real captured logs rather than inferred:
168	
169	1. **The Stop hook's `hooklog` line** — `<iso> run=<id> Stop: done exit=<n>
170	   <reason>`. It reaches the transcript because `hooklog` mirrors to stderr and
171	   the harness records hook stderr (as an `isMeta` feedback turn, a
172	   `stop_hook_summary`, or a `hook_success` attachment). This is the **only**
173	   mark a *passing* run leaves, which is what makes work-scope run counts — not
174	   merely failure counts — possible at all. Its `reason` distinguishes the four
175	   outcomes the hook itself declares: `checks-passed`, `blocking-findings`,
176	   `loop-guard-relent` (blocking findings that survived two fix attempts — a
177	   failure that prints no findings block, readable *only* here), and
178	   `runner-error` (the checks did not run, an anti-win that would otherwise
179	   masquerade as a quiet clean day).
180	2. **`report-findings`' summary line** — `N blocking, M advisory (<scope>
181	   scope: …)`. It names its own scope and survives the `| tail` an agent
182	   usually pipes a run through. It is printed *only* when there were findings,
183	   so it counts failures and finding volume — never runs.
184	3. **The runner's invocation in a Bash command** (`node …/check_the_world.mjs`).
185	   This is how the world scope runs at all: its Stop-hook sibling does not
186	   exist, because the world sweep is wired into the test/CI flow rather than
187	   the hook (`engine/checks/README.md`, "Enforcement wiring").
188	
189	**CI counts when the agent was in the loop on it.** Write, commit, let CI run,
190	fix what it caught is the same correction loop as the Stop hook's, one turn
191	wider, so a CI check failure the session acted on is the same kind of win. It
192	is counted exactly when the session **pulled the job log in** — which is what
193	"the agent was in the loop" means operationally, and it draws the line the
194	owner asked for: a nightly or post-merge run nobody looked at stays uncounted,
195	correctly, because nothing was corrected. Two things follow, and both are
196	mechanism, not policy:
197	
198	- CI logs arrive through a CI-log tool rather than Bash (matched by name shape
199	  — `job_logs` / `run_logs` / `workflow_logs` — so a different MCP server or a
200	  rename still lands), and every line carries the Actions timestamp in front of
201	  the command's own output, so each mark tolerates that prefix. Without it a
202	  fetched CI log reads as having printed nothing.
203	- A job log can be fetched repeatedly while iterating on the failure, and
204	  nothing in a fetch says *which run* it was. So CI texts dedupe on the check
205	  output itself: two fetches of one job are identical and collapse; two real
206	  runs differ by their Actions timestamps at least. Two genuinely identical
207	  runs collapse too — an under-count, the direction this counter is allowed to
208	  be wrong in.
209	
210	From those, per bucket:
211	
212	- **`checks`**, keyed by scope (`work` / `world`): `runs` — observed
213	  activations; `failures` — the subset that reported at least one blocking
214	  finding; `errors` — runs where the runner could not launch; `blocking` /
215	  `advisory` — finding *volume* summed over those runs. A rule blocking in two
216	  consecutive runs counts twice: the question is how often the checks caught
217	  something, not how many distinct problems existed. Plus `ciRuns` /
218	  `ciFailures`, the **subset** of those that came from a fetched CI log —
219	  carried separately because that source can only see a run that printed
220	  something (a green CI sweep prints nothing and is invisible), so a consumer
221	  wanting a rate over runs it can see the whole of subtracts them, while one
222	  asking "how often did the checks catch something" uses the totals.
223	- **`checkFindings`**, keyed by rule id, `{ blocking, advisory }` — read off
224	  each rendered `[BLOCKING] <rule>  <file>` header. Lossier than the summary
225	  totals (a run piped through `tail -3` keeps the summary and drops the
226	  headers), which is why both are kept: a gap between them *is* the truncation,
227	  visible rather than assumed away.
228	
229	Runs are counted only from the marks a passing run also leaves — hook
230	completion lines, and Bash invocations — never from the summary line. Where a
231	runner ran without its command naming it (a `make test` step wrapping it), the
232	summary lines in its output are the floor: the count is the **max** of the two
233	signals, never their sum, because they are two views of the same runs.
234	
235	Two things keep this honest and must stay stated wherever the numbers are read:
236	
237	- **Only Bash and CI-log tool results count**, paired back to their `tool_use`.
238	  In the corpus that owns the runners, reading a file that merely *contains*
239	  this vocabulary is the ordinary case, not a corner one.
240	- **These are floors, never over-counts.** A sweep whose CI log nobody fetched
241	  left no mark in any transcript. A hook killed before it logged left none
242	  either. A green CI run prints nothing to be seen by. The bias is
243	  one-directional by construction, which is the direction that keeps "the
244	  checks caught N things this week" a claim worth making.
245	
246	One hook execution is recorded under two entry shapes (the feedback turn the
247	model sees, and the harness's `stop_hook_summary` repeating the same stderr).
248	They dedupe on the `hooklog` stamps the text carries — the one identity stable
249	across both shapes and unique per execution. Counting both would double every
250	failure, which is precisely the number that must not be inflated.
251	
252	Zeros are implicit everywhere: a mounted skill with no loads simply has no
253	key. Consumers derive the zero set by diffing against the repo's mounted
254	skills (pack registry for a member; for the fleet view, each member's declared
255	packs), which is what makes "never loads" visible at all.
256	
257	## 5. The per-repo aggregate — `.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json`
258	
259	Written by **`usage-fold`**: an agentless daily task of `grow_with_claudinite`
260	(deterministic preprocessing, no agent, cheapest possible run), outcome
261	`merged-pr` — the worker opens a PR with the regenerated file and arms
262	auto-merge; a byte-identical recompute opens nothing. It lives under
263	`.claudinite/local/` because that is the repo-owned area the vendoring refresh
264	never touches — the mount root itself is read-only canon.
265	
266	Two tiers, per the owner's fast-insight requirement:
267	
268	- **Days** (short term): keyed by the capture filename's UTC date. A file's
269	  stamp is its push moment, so day *D* gains files only during *D* and is
270	  immutable once *D* ends. While a day is inside the raw retention window, the
271	  fold recomputes it **from scratch from the live files, every run** — no
272	  ingest ledger, no double-count risk, and a counting-bug fix self-heals the
273	  whole visible window on its next run. Day rows older than the window drop
274	  out of the file (their content lives on in their week row).
275	- **Weeks** (long term): ISO-8601 weeks, append-once via a single
276	  **`foldedThrough` watermark**. Each run, every completed day *d* with
277	  `foldedThrough < d < today` is added into its week and the mark advances.
278	  Days close strictly in order, so a monotone mark is the entire exactly-once
279	  mechanism. Days fold at day+1 — long before their raw files die — so the
280	  pipeline tolerates ~`retention_days − 1` consecutive days of task outage
281	  before losing anything; past that, the loss is **visible, never silent**:
282	  each week row records how many days it absorbed (`days: 5` declares its own
283	  hole).
284	
285	```json
286	{
287	  "version": 1,
288	  "foldedThrough": "2026-07-26",
289	  "days": {
290	    "2026-07-28": { "captures": 3, "merges": 2, "sessions": 2,
291	                    "userMessages": 31, "userCommands": 4,
292	                    "skillLoads": { "merge-to-main": 1 },
293	                    "checks": {
294	                      "work":  { "runs": 34, "failures": 12, "errors": 0, "blocking": 15,
295	                                 "advisory": 0, "ciRuns": 0, "ciFailures": 0 },
296	                      "world": { "runs": 42, "failures": 3, "errors": 0, "blocking": 5,
297	                                 "advisory": 131, "ciRuns": 1, "ciFailures": 1 }
298	                    },
299	                    "checkFindings": { "task-lifecycle": { "blocking": 8, "advisory": 0 } } }
300	  },
301	  "weeks": {
302	    "2026-W30": { "days": 7, "captures": 11, "merges": 9, "sessionDays": 8,
303	                  "userMessages": 210, "userCommands": 23,
304	                  "skillLoads": { "merge-to-main": 6 },
305	                  "checks": { "work": { "runs": 190, "failures": 51, "errors": 0, "blocking": 66,
306	                                        "advisory": 3, "ciRuns": 0, "ciFailures": 0 } },
307	                  "checkFindings": { "task-lifecycle": { "blocking": 40, "advisory": 0 } } }
308	  }
309	}
310	```
311	
312	Keys are sorted for stable diffs. All counters sum exactly under folding —
313	except distinct-session counts, which do not (a session spanning two days is
314	distinct in each). Weeks therefore carry **`sessionDays`** — the sum of the
315	day-level distinct counts — named for what it is rather than pretending to a
316	precision folding cannot give.
317	
318	Frozen weeks are a stated trade, not a surprise: a counting bug found later
319	heals the day window automatically, but weeks folded under the old counting
320	keep it — re-freezing would need raw data the retention TTL deliberately
321	destroyed. Git history records which commit folded what, so the boundary is
322	auditable. The same trade applies to a *new* counter: weeks folded before the
323	check counts existed carry no `checks` key, and the fold extends them from the
324	day they close forward rather than refusing to advance the watermark past them
325	— a partial series beats a wedged one, and the boundary is visible in the file.
326	
327	Precondition: the `conversationLogs` signal reports the branch present. Runs
328	where nothing changed are no-ops (no PR), and the agentless run costs seconds.
329	
330	## 6. The fleet aggregate — `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json`
331	
332	Written by **`fleet-usage`**: an agentless daily task of the **sheepdog**
333	pack, alongside `fleet-census` and `fleet-freshness` and shaped exactly like
334	them — the sweep (`aggregate-fleet-usage.mjs`, inside the task's folder) *is*
335	the `agent_preprocessing`, `required_secrets` asks for `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`,
336	and members are enumerated via `fleet-api.mjs` from the sheepdog config entry.
337	It runs only where the sheepdog pack is declared — the fleet-enforcer repo.
338	
339	The aggregation is a **stateless full recompute**: read each member's
340	`.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json` at its default branch over REST (one
341	file per member, no clones), and rebuild the fleet file as a pure function of
342	the inputs. Stateless recompute is idempotent by definition and self-heals any
343	past error; at this cardinality (~repos × skills × weeks, all small) there is
344	nothing to optimize.
345	
346	- **Grain**: full (week × repo × skill, and week × repo × **rule**) for
347	  history, plus the members' current day windows verbatim for the fast view —
348	  "what happened this week?" at day-grain, trends at week-grain. Nothing
349	  pre-summed. The checks are carried at the same grain and for the same reason
350	  as the skill loads: whether a rule earns its place is a fleet-shaped
351	  question. A rule that never fires in one repo may simply not be that repo's
352	  subject; a rule that never fires in **any** of them is mis-described or
353	  worthless — and a rule that keeps firing everywhere is the corpus's
354	  best-performing guard. Only a view across every member tells those apart.
355	- **Coverage is explicit**: a member without the usage file (not yet folding)
356	  or with an unreadable one is listed in a `coverage` section as absent —
357	  census-style, never silently skipped — so gaps in the denominators are
358	  visible rather than baked in. A member still on an older fold (no `checks`
359	  key) lands as an empty check row rather than an exception: the sweep leads
360	  the members' upgrades, so that is the normal state for a while.
361	- **A `_note` field** states the sampling population: captured sessions only —
362	  merging sessions plus sessions that ended cleanly enough for the SessionEnd
363	  hook. Reclaimed containers and crashes are invisible. The file must not read
364	  as a census. The note carries the checks' second, narrower boundary too: the
365	  counts are what a *session* saw, so a world sweep that ran in CI is not in
366	  them, and every check number is a floor on activations.
367	- Outcome `merged-pr` (owner decision): the sweep opens a PR on a run-stamped
368	  branch in the enforcer repo and arms auto-merge. This keeps the write inside
369	  the outcome taxonomy `verify-outcome.mjs` enforces, lets the enforcer's CI
370	  gate a malformed file, and makes the daily PR stream a browsable audit trail.
371	  A byte-identical recompute opens nothing.
372	
373	## 7. Consumers — who learns from this
374	
375	- **The owner**, ad hoc: both files are small sorted JSON on tracked branches —
376	  readable in the GitHub UI, over MCP, or via `git show`, with full history.
377	- **Canon curation** (the promote run): the empirical feedback the rung-4/5
378	  routing decision currently lacks, in both directions. Never loads across the
379	  fleet ⇒ the trigger is mis-described, or the content should not be gated at
380	  all (rules wearing a skill's clothes); always loads ⇒ likewise not
381	  activity-scoped. Raw counts alone cannot distinguish healthy-rare from
382	  broken — a version-bump skill loading rarely is fine — which is why the
383	  denominators exist: the metric is loads against the sessions where the
384	  skill's own declared trigger plausibly applied.
385	- **Canon curation, on the rules** (the same run): the checks' half answers a
386	  sharper question than the skills' half, because a check failure is an
387	  observed correction rather than an inferred one. A rule with steady failures
388	  across the fleet is a guard earning its keep and an argument for converting
389	  more prose into checks (`prose-to-checks`); a rule that has never fired
390	  anywhere is either unreachable or describing something that does not happen;
391	  a rule firing on nearly every run is a *default the corpus should change*
392	  rather than a violation worth blocking on. `errors` reads differently from
393	  all three: it means enforcement was silently off, and it is the one number
394	  here whose right value is zero.
395	- **Sheepdog's fleet tasks**, later: freshness-style drift issues citing the
396	  fleet file ("skill X: 0 loads fleet-wide in 6 weeks"). The learning loop
397	  stays in the enforcer's domain, not the canon's. Out of scope here; noted so
398	  the file's grain is chosen for it (it is).
399	
400	## 8. TTLs, end to end
401	
402	| data | where | TTL |
403	|---|---|---|
404	| transcript | harness config dir | harness-owned (ephemeral in cloud sessions) |
405	| raw capture `.jsonl` | `conversation-logs` branch | `retention_days` (unchanged; unset ⇒ capture-only, no prune) |
406	| day rows | member usage file | the raw window — then their week row carries them |
407	| week rows | member usage file | indefinite (~KBs/year; revisit only if a file nears 1 MB) |
408	| fleet file | enforcer repo | none needed — derived; history is git's |
409	
410	## 9. Failure modes, stated
411	
412	- **Fold outage** longer than ~`retention_days − 1` days: unfolded days lose
413	  their raw backing. The hole is visible (week's `days` count short), never a
414	  silently wrong number.
415	- **Hook never fires** (reclaim, crash): the record degrades exactly to
416	  today's merge-only capture. No consumer breaks.
417	- **Scrub boundary** (unchanged from capture's existing statement): a secret
418	  the session itself transformed is invisible to any static scrub; the branch
419	  shares the repo's access control and push protection stays the last net.
420	- **A member goes quiet**: its day window empties, its weeks stop growing, and
421	  the fleet file shows it with zeros-by-absence plus its last folded week —
422	  distinguishable from "not folding" via the `coverage` section.
423	- **A check ran where no session saw it** (a CI run nobody fetched the log for,
424	  a hook killed before it logged, a green CI sweep that printed nothing): the
425	  run is simply not counted. This is the one under-count the design accepts by
426	  construction, and it is one-directional — the numbers are floors, never
427	  inflated. Stated in the fleet file's own `_note` so a consumer cannot read
428	  them as a census of enforcement. Detached CI is *deliberately* out: the
429	  metric is about the correction loop, and a run nobody looked at corrected
430	  nothing.
431	- **The harness changes how it records hooks**: the marks in §4.1 are harness
432	  output, not a contract Claudinite owns. A shape change makes check counts
433	  fall to zero — loudly, since a repo with checks wired cannot plausibly report
434	  no activations — rather than drift quietly wrong. Each mark is read by one
435	  exported function with a fixture copied from a real capture, so re-pinning is
436	  a fixture update, not an investigation.
437	
438	## 10. Decisions on record (owner, 2026-07-28)
439	
440	1. **Two tiers, days + weeks** — days for insight faster than a week, matched
441	   to the 10-day raw TTL; weeks as the long-term series, aggregated from days.
442	2. **Days statelessly recomputed; weeks append-once from days** — the
443	   watermark replaces any ingest ledger.
444	3. **Denominators include sessions and user commands**, alongside captures,
445	   merges, and user messages.
446	4. **Fleet awareness is the sheepdog domain** — the canon must not know
447	   specific member repos; the aggregate lands in the fleet-enforcer repo via
448	   its pack's tasks.
449	5. **Auto-merged daily PR, not a direct commit**, for the GENERATED aggregate
450	   writes — into the enforcer repo, and by extension the member fold.
451	6. **SessionEnd capture is a welcome best-effort bonus**, contingent on
452	   double-write safety being proven first (§3.1's tests), with `issue-0`
453	   naming for issueless captures.
454	7. **No migration plan** — the existing convergence machinery carries the
455	   rollout; ordering is handled by shipping §3 in one PR (§3.4).
456	
457	### Owner, 2026-07-29
458	
459	8. **Check activations and check failures are counted too** (§4.1), at both
460	   levels — per repo in the fold, and fleet-wide in the sheepdog sweep, exactly
461	   as the skill loads are. **Failures are the point**: when a check fails the
462	   agent corrects immediately, so a failure is a win, and every one is counted.
463	   Executions are counted as far as the transcript allows and the shortfall is
464	   stated rather than papered over (§9) — the numbers are floors.
465	9. **Per-rule grain is kept**, not just per-scope totals: "which rule catches
466	   things" is what the promote run and `prose-to-checks` actually need, and it
467	   is what the fleet view exists to answer across members.
468	10. **CI counts when it was part of the agent loop** — write, commit, let CI
469	    run, fix what it caught — and not otherwise. Operationally: the session
470	    pulled the job log in. A nightly or post-merge run nobody looked at is
471	    explicitly *not crucial* and stays uncounted, because nothing was
472	    corrected. The CI share is carried separately (`ciRuns` / `ciFailures`)
473	    since that source sees only runs that printed.
474
